beats.text: It was a merchant's mark, centuries before email.
beats.note: It meant 'at the rate of': three crates @ two shillings. A trader's shorthand for a price, not a piece of computer punctuation.

beats.name: Francesco Lapi
beats.role: A Florentine merchant wrote the earliest known @ (standing in for an amphora, a unit of wine) in a letter about treasure the conquistadors shipped from Peru. In Spanish and Portuguese the sign is still 'arroba,' a unit of weight.

beats.text: @ had sat on typewriter keyboards since the 1880s.
beats.note: Little used, always there. Which is exactly why it was free for the taking when networks needed a character that would never turn up inside someone's name.

beats.text: Ray Tomlinson grabbed @ to split the name from the machine.
beats.note: It was not an assignment: he was fooling around with ARPANET. He needed one symbol to mean this user at this computer, and @ already meant at. The address bar has looked that way ever since.

beats.text: A mark for pricing wine now sits in New York's Museum of Modern Art, credited to Tomlinson.

beats.line: @ meant 'at this price' for four centuries before 'at this computer.'
